title: Two Sum on sorted array: left+right pointer, O(1) space.
shortTitle: Two Sum on a Sorted Array: Left and Right Pointers, O(1) Space
keyPoints: Two opposite-end pointers find a pair summing to the target in O(n) time and O(1) space on a sorted array.
If the sum is less than the target, move the left pointer up to increase the sum; if greater, move the right pointer down.
Correctness: when the sum is too small, the left value cannot contribute even with the largest remaining value, so it is safely discarded.
The precondition is that the array must be sorted; on unsorted data, use a HashMap approach instead.
Watch for integer overflow on large amounts: use long or BigDecimal in real financial code.
Each pointer only moves inward and they never cross back, so the entire array is scanned at most once.
Return -1 or an empty result when no valid pair exists.

s1_definition.oneliner: On sorted data, two opposite-end pointers find a target pair in one linear pass with zero extra memory.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two-pointer technique** – a `left` pointer starts at the smallest value and a `right` pointer at the largest in a sorted array.
- **Decision rule** – if `a[left] + a[right] < target`, increment `left`; if greater, decrement `right`; if equal, return the pair.
- **O(n) time, O(1) space** – each pointer moves at most n steps total, and no extra data structure is needed.
- **Sorted precondition** – the array must be sorted for the pointer movement reasoning to be correct.
- **Alternative** – on unsorted data, use a `HashMap` approach at the cost of O(n) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh at the National Bank of India has a sorted list of past deposit amounts and wants to know which two deposits together equal a disputed figure. He puts one finger on the smallest deposit and one on the largest. If their total is too small he slides the low finger up; if too big he slides the high finger down. He finds the pair without writing a side list of everything he has seen.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two Sum on a sorted array finds two values that add up to a target using opposite-end two pointers, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Place a left pointer on the smallest value and a right pointer on the largest. If their sum is less than the target, move left up; if greater, move right down; if equal, return the pair.

The correctness argument is the part interviewers want to hear. Because the array is sorted, when the current sum is too small, the smallest value can never contribute to a valid pair even alongside the largest remaining value, so you can safely discard it by advancing the left pointer, and the mirror image holds when the sum is too large.

The trade-off against the HashMap version is memory. The HashMap approach works on unsorted data in linear time but needs O(n) extra space, while the sorted two-pointer approach needs no extra space but requires the input to already be sorted.

In a banking project at the National Bank of India, the reconciliation service uses this to check whether a disputed charge equals the sum of two legitimate debits, working in BigDecimal so there is never a rounding error.

Remember one sentence: On a sorted array, two opposite-end pointers find a target-sum pair in O(n) time and O(1) space by discarding the smaller value when the sum is too small and the larger when too large.
